doc.title: J. Leo Rayhill interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 23, 2007

title: Harry James and Stan Kenton late in life
summary: Ailing Harry James played his heart out; he rescued Kenton after Kenton's stroke at Saratoga.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: It’s really great. And Harry James was here and it was shortly before he died — and he went up to the Onondaga Golf and Country Club and played and he was unreal. His face was haggard and you could see that he was in the last throes of cancer, and he played his heart out. He was great. Those guys, like Bob Scobey who I’ve played many times on the show, there was a pillar that — he played at this club and he needed the pillar to support himself up while he played. But he played great. And down at Saratoga they had a big band carnival and Harry James was on it and Stan Kenton was on it and anyway Stan Kenton had had his stroke. He’d had that fall. And he got up before the audience and he was playing well. That was the surprising thing. He could play the piano all right but he couldn’t remember the members when he went to introduce the members of his band. And just from out in the wing Harry James came out, put his arm around him and talked on and got right out of the tough hole he was in. I always thought that was class.
